opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most exciting directions, and also one where I try to hold two ideas at once.

On the optimistic side, biology is incredibly data-rich in ways language isn't. You've got genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, imaging, longitudinal clinical records, wearables. Each of these captures a slice of what's actually going on in a person, and historically we've built narrow, specialist models for each one. What's changed is that we now have architectures that can, at least in principle, take in many modalities and learn shared representations across them. We've seen glimpses of this already. Protein structure models, single-cell foundation models, and medical imaging models that generalize better than anything we had a few years ago. So the idea that you could have a system that reasons fluently across a patient's genome, their pathology slides, and their clinical notes, and connects those to the scientific literature, doesn't feel like science fiction anymore.

That said, I'd push back a little on the assumption that the path is just "add more modalities to a big model and it'll figure it out." There are a few real challenges.

One is data. A lot of biological data is siloed, small relative to web text, noisy, and collected under very different protocols. Labels are expensive, and ground truth is often fuzzy. Two labs can measure the "same" thing and get meaningfully different distributions.

Another is evaluation. In language we can check whether an answer is right fairly quickly. In biology, the real test of whether a model has learned something meaningful is often a wet-lab experiment or a clinical outcome years later. That feedback loop is slow and expensive, so it's easy to fool yourself with benchmarks that don't reflect real-world utility.

And then there's the question of whether deep integration is even the right abstraction versus tool use. One thing I find compelling is that a strong general reasoning model may not need to natively "see" every modality. It might be more effective to orchestrate specialist models, call the right analysis pipelines, and interpret the results, much like a good physician-scientist does. I suspect the answer ends up being a mix: native integration where the modality is rich and central, like imaging, and tool-mediated integration for highly specialized data.

Where I'm most hopeful is that language models give us a kind of connective tissue. Language is how science communicates hypotheses, results, and uncertainty. If you can ground biological representations in that, you get systems that don't just predict but can explain and propose experiments, and that collaborate with researchers. That's where I think the real acceleration comes from.

And of course, because this is health, safety and rigor have to scale with capability. The bar isn't "impressive demo," it's "does this reliably help patients and scientists without introducing new harms." That keeps you honest about the progress.

r001.rationale: The response says newer architectures can take in many modalities and learn shared representations across them, presenting this capability as part of its optimistic case.

r002.rationale: It recommends different integration approaches for imaging and specialized data, but does not say how long integration will take or that the time will vary by modality.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that I'm very optimistic about the direction, but I've become more sober about the timeline and the mechanics of how it actually happens.

Let me separate two things. There's the question of whether language models can reason about biology, which they increasingly can, because so much of biomedical knowledge is encoded in text. That's what we saw with Med-PaLM and the work that followed. And then there's the harder question you're asking, which is about actually integrating the raw modalities: genomics, proteomics, imaging, time-series physiological signals, single-cell data, and so on. Those are not text, they're not even close to text, and the inductive biases that make transformers great at language don't automatically transfer.

What makes me optimistic is that we've seen the playbook work in adjacent domains. Vision got folded into language models once we had a good encoder and enough paired data to align the representations. Protein structure is a good example of a biological modality where a dedicated model, AlphaFold, gave us an interpretable, high-quality representation that you can then plug into a broader system. So I think the path is less "one giant model that natively ingests everything" and more a set of strong domain encoders whose outputs a general reasoning model learns to use.

The bottleneck, frankly, is data, and specifically the paired data. You need the genomic sequence alongside the phenotype, the retinal image alongside the outcome, the longitudinal EHR alongside the lab values, all linked and consented and cleaned. That data exists in fragments across health systems and biobanks, but it's small by modern pretraining standards and it's siloed for legitimate privacy reasons. So a lot of the real progress is unglamorous infrastructure and governance work rather than architecture work.

The other thing I'd flag is evaluation. In medicine especially, it's easy to get a model that looks impressive on a benchmark and still isn't trustworthy in the way a clinician needs. When you add modalities, you compound that problem, because now the model can be subtly wrong about the image or the signal in ways that a text-only evaluation never catches. So I'd want to see grounding, calibrated uncertainty, and the ability to say "I don't know" built in from the start rather than bolted on.

But if you ask whether I think this is going to happen in a meaningful way over the next several years, yes. The scientific payoff is enormous, because biology is exactly the kind of domain where the knowledge is distributed across modalities that no single human can hold in their head at once. That's where a model that can actually bridge them has a chance to tell us something we didn't already know.

r001.rationale: The candidate is optimistic because biology’s knowledge is distributed across modalities, and says a model that can bridge them could produce new insights.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the overall timeline is less certain, but does not say integration time will vary across biological modalities.

astra-6.text:
I’m pretty optimistic about it. Language captures a lot of what we know about biology, but it’s a pretty lossy representation. There’s so much information in sequences, imaging, and measurements of how cells respond to different interventions that isn’t fully captured in a paper or a textbook. Being able to learn directly from those modalities could give models a much richer understanding.

The hard part is getting those sources of information to connect. You want more than a model that can separately understand an image and answer a question about genetics. You want it to use both together to make a prediction that it couldn’t make from either alone. That requires good data linking measurements across those different scales, and careful evaluation of whether the model has actually learned something useful.

The possibility I find especially exciting is closing the loop with experiments: a model helps propose an experiment, you run it, and the results improve the model’s understanding. There’s a lot of work between here and there, but that seems like a promising path toward systems that help us discover new biology.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about learning directly from biological modalities and says combining them can enable predictions neither modality could support alone.

r002.rationale: The response mentions work still needed, but does not state that integration timelines will vary across biological modalities.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m pretty optimistic. Biology has all these different ways of observing the same underlying system—DNA sequences, gene expression, protein structures, images of cells—and each gives you a partial view. The exciting possibility is that a model trained across those modalities could learn connections that are hard to see when you study each one independently.

But integration alone isn’t enough. You need data that meaningfully connects those views, and you need to test whether the model can predict what happens when you intervene. Can it tell you how a particular change will affect a cell, or which experiment would resolve an uncertainty? That’s a much stronger standard than doing well on a static benchmark.

So I think there’s a lot of potential here, especially in a loop where models help propose experiments and the results improve the models. The real measure of progress will be whether that loop helps us discover things we wouldn’t otherwise have found.

r001.rationale: The response says a model trained across biological modalities could learn connections that are hard to see when studying each modality independently, identifying cross-modal combination as a reason for optimism.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that integration timelines will vary across biological modalities.
